title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
In the following report, I will be investigating commuting patterns by race/ethnicity via public transportation in New Jersey, and ask which counties and ethnicities are measured most and least reliably. Since I will specifically be paying attention to margin of error, I cannot directly calculate percentage of people who commute via public transportation, and so will rely on the absolute number and will use total commuters by race/ethnicity as a point of comparison.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories
Given that we have two divisions of our data (1) total commuters and (2) public transportation users, which carry very different spreads of reliability, I decided to use two different reliability scales across races/ethnicity.
To choose cutoffs for categories, I looked at two histograms of the data:

moe_p_ttl <- c(county_data$moe_p_ttl_white, county_data$moe_p_ttl_black, county_data$moe_p_ttl_asian, county_data$moe_p_ttl_hisp)

moe_p_ttl_hist <- hist(moe_p_ttl, col="orange",main="MOE Percentage (Total)", breaks = seq(0,40, 2))







moe_p_transp <- c(county_data$moe_p_transp_white, county_data$moe_p_transp_black, county_data$moe_p_transp_asian, county_data$moe_p_transp_hisp)

moe_p_transp_hist <- hist(moe_p_transp, col="blue",main="MOE Percentage (Transportation)", breaks = seq(0,600, 20))








As we can see in (1), the margin of error ratio (in percent) for all commuters (combined), is relatively right-skewed, with most of the data below 10. It therefore seems justifiable to create the following categories: - < 10 = High confidence - < 20 = Moderate confidence (I chose 8 as there is generally a major increase after 8%) - > 20 = Low confidence
For (2), which is also right-skewed, and has an outlier at 600, it seems justifiable to have the following categories - < 40 = High confidence - < 80 = Medium confidence - < 80 = Low confidence

#Total White categories
county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability_ttl_white = case_when(
    moe_p_ttl_white < 10  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_p_ttl_white < 20 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Reliability of counties differs both between and within race and ethnicity. As can be seen in the charts above, there is the highest reliability of white commuters – both total and public transit. However, when looking at white public transportation riders, the number of counties with low confidence jumps to 8 counties and high confidence plummets by 9 counties. While there is high confidence for total Black commuters in 16 out of 21 counties, this confidence drops to only 11 counties for those who commute via public transportation. Asian and Hispanic/Latino show similar trends, with each also dropping in counties with high confidence and gaining in moderate and low confidence.

section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this, I compared the average population of counties in each reliability category.
I used group_by by county and reliability per race/ethnicity, and summarized by average population in order to isolate just the average populations and count for each confidence level. I then arranged it by average population in descending order in order to better assess the change in decreasing average populations to confidence levels.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The fact that smaller counties have lower confidence in their data being accurate can have serious consequences for policy. As can be seen in the charts above, smaller counties like Salem, Cape May, and Warren have lower confidence levels across the ethnicity/race and rider type spectrum; on the other hand, more populated counties, such as Bergen, Middlesex, and Essex, have consistently high confidence levels. When creating commuter policy for the state, residents of Bergen County are more likely to be better served as we have more complete data for them and therefore can more accurately assess their needs. On the other hand, since we have a less accurate understanding of who Salem residents are, we are left more in the dark as to how to assist them. A similar logic carries over by race; since there are more white residents within each county of New Jersey, we can have much higher confidence in the ACS data; on the other hand, since there are far fewer Asian residents, we are unable to rely upon just the ACS to give us guidance to meet their needs. For example, if we were to explore a policy aimed at increasing ridership among Asian commuters in Hunterdon County, where there are an estimated 22 Asian residents and a margin of error of 31, but we only relied on the estimated data and ignored the margin of error, we could end up over-funding in an area in which there are actually no Asian residents at all. On the other hand, in Gloucester County, where there is estimated 160 Asian residents, a margin of error of 140, and low confidence, we could end up either overfunding an areas in which there are actually 20 Asian residents, or under-funding by 87.5% if there were actually 300 Asian residents. The ACS is therefore an excellent tool to get a base understanding of demographics across regions, but it must be used with other outside resource, as on its own it can under- or over-predict for smaller population areas or vulnerable populations.

title: Assignment 3: Margin of Error in Poverty in Philadelphia
text:
##Introduction
In a recent article published to WHYY and Philly.com, Alfred Lubrano reported that the US ACS 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 five-year estimates showed a sharp increase in inequality, measured in percent in poverty and median household income, between certain neighborhoods. He found that poverty increased and median househoold income decreased across multiple neighborhoods. The most drastic changes can be seen in the the following neighborhoods:


Show code
library(readr)
WHYY_data <- read_csv("assignments/WHYY_data.csv")
View(WHYY_data)


As can be seen from his data, Eastwick saw the highest percentage point increase in poverty rate – from 12 to 14. Germantown, with a absolute $33,089 loss, saw the most drastic decrease in median household income across the period. On the other hand, Schuylkill-SW Center City saw the largest percentage point decrease in poverty rate, from 21 to 10%, as well as the highest absolute income increase, with it spiking by about $31,000. These show a grow a growing income divide in Philadelphia, with the gap between the poorest and wealthiest neighborhoods getting larger.
He separately reported also using the 2015-2016 and 2016-2017 one-year estimate that percent of white people in poverty skyrocketed from “14.8% to 19.4% between 2016 and 2017.” Using the 2013-2017 5-year ACS, he cites poverty rates among white residents of Holmesburg have jumped from 2% to 19% in the period.
These results are alarming and disturbing. They also need to be subject to further scrutiny if we are to make policy surrounding where to allocate limited city resources to address growing needs among the populace. Specifically, they need to take margin of error into account, as if they don’t we could end up over- or under-allocating to the wrong neighborhoods. For example, according to Lubrano’s analysis, Powelton, Hunting Park, and Mantua have the highest percent in poverty in the 2013-2017 survey and are all relatively equal. It would therefore make sense to focus allocation of further city resources to these areas; however, should we account for margin of error and find that one has the potential to be 10+ percentage points higher than another, it may affect our decision-making.
This report will therefore attempt to fill in these gaps on the census tract level so that we can better track where percent poverty and median household income has changed throughout the city – both in total and by race – so that we can better plan for future allocation of city resources to the most vulnerable regions.

##1 Locating our Data


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)


First, we will download the same data that Lubrano relied on for his analysis, but by census tract:

5-year: 2006-2010 and 2013-2017

Total poverty rate
White poverty rate
median household income

1-year: 2016-2017

White poverty rate (countywide)


We are using census tracts as neighborhood boundaries are not official and can often be disputed; on the other hand, census tracts are standardized by the Federal Government. One issue here though is that census tract boundaries also change, so this may affect our results.
Second, the analyses for 5-year changes have a 3-year gap in between their windows and therefore do not overlap; we can can therefore compare them with each other. However, the 1-year estimates overlap with the latter 5-year window. It is therefore best to analyze these separately as it does not take every year (2013-2015) into account.
Third, the author does not specify whether for change median household income he adjusted for inflation. For this exercise, we will not adjust for inflation.
Finally, the article does not state what their metric for “poverty” is. Is he looking at below 100%, 100-149%, or at or above 150%? For sake of ease, we will be using tables that ignore these percentages.
Note that while the author looked specifically at “majority-white neighborhoods,” we will consider all census tracts, regardless whether they are majority white.
First, we will get total population, total poverty, white population, white poverty, and median household income information for 2013-2017. We can also add columns for percent in poverty and the margin of error for this percent using moe_prop():


Show code

    )

##2 Testing our data
We tested whether the change was statistically distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence. In other words, we chekced in which tracts does the margin of error not cross 0.

#3 Adjudicating the Article
The central claim of the article, that there is growing inequality, does not seem to have support. As the charts show below, when we look at the 50 census tracts with the (statistically significant) highest and lowest poverty rates, the highest poverty rate census tracts have actually decreased in rate and the lowest poverty rate census tracts have increased in poverty rate. In other words, the poorest tracts have become less poor and the wealthiest tracts have become less wealthy. The charts for highest and lowest median household income show a similar pattern; both the (statistically significant) poorest 25 and wealthiest 25 are overwhelmingly gaining in income (not adjusted for inflation).
The exception is white poverty, which does seem to align with the article’s claim, as (statistically significant) census tracts with high white poverty do seem to be increasing drastically (and with margin of error, perhaps even more) across the city.
Note though that these analyses are limited as we did not take into consideration inflation or neighborhoods (as the article did not supply their methodology behind boundaries). The article also hypothesized potential reasons leading to an increase in white poverty, such as the recession and drugs, but offered no evidence to support this. A more detailed investigation that takes spatial statistics into account therefore seems warranted.

#4 Rewriting
In dull and opaque detail, the new 2018 5-year ACS leaves most of its effects on Philadelphia relatively undetermined. Rigorous analysis revealed that only 20% of census tracts in the city allow for reporters to definitively understand whether poverty rates and incomes actually increased or decreased in them. Of those 20%, inequality seems to either be slowing down or reversing (possibly a sign of gentrification), and white poverty seems to be growing or shrinking across the city.
